newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls against German mark, Japanese yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls against German mark, Japanese yen.

text.p: The dollar fell from its highest level in nearly three years against the mark Tuesday as the German currency was bolstered by a sharp drop in the Italian lira and British pound.
The dollar rallied against the Japanese yen overseas but then faltered in U.S. trading.

Mounting fears that Italy will not be a member of the first group of European nations forming a single currency and fading expectations for the Bank of England to raise interest rates caused the currencies of those nations to drop sharply.
Dealers bought marks in order to sell lira and the pound, thus strengthening the mark versus the dollar.

"We're seeing strong, significant purchases of marks against periphery countries in Europe such as Italy and Spain and also against sterling," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.
"Those mark purchases are the equivalent of dollar sales," he said.

After reaching 1.7050 marks, its highest level in 34 months, the dollar fell to 1.6850 marks by the end of U.S. trading from 1.7015 in late European trading on Monday. The U.S. market was closed on Monday for the Presidents Day holiday.
The dollar also retreated from a three-year high against the Swiss franc, closing at 1.47 compared with 1.4810 francs on Monday.

Traders speculated that Japanese authorities were ready to intervene in the currency market, buying yen for dollars, in order to keep the dollar below the critical level of 125 yen. This sentiment capped the dollar's gains, dealers said.
The dollar fell to 123.90 yen from 124.35 in late European trade on Monday. The dollar hit a high of 124.71 yen during Tuesday's trading, a bit below its recent high of 124.82 yen.
The British pound fell to $1.6081 from $1.6170.

The pound weakened after Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Monday that a spate of British economic data, along with the currency's recent strength, had diminished the need for an imminent interest rate rise.
The dollar strengthened recently on mounting fears over the health of China's paramount leader, 92-year-old Deng Xiaoping, as traders bought dollars as a perceived safe haven.
China on Tuesday played down fears over the health of Xiaoping, which were raised after Communist Party Chief Jiang Zemin cut short an out-of-town trip to visit the ailing leader.

"The dollar rallied late in European trade on Monday and remained high. Only a minor extension of this dollar rally was made when the Xiaoping news hit," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The lira was hurt by comments from Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and reported newspaper remarks from Belgian central bank chief Alfonse Verplaetse.

Prodi said on Monday that Germany was less committed to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) than Italy, fuelling rumours Bonn was conspiring to keep the lira out of the first wave of nations joining the single currency.

Verplaetse denied a report in a Belgian newspaper, which quoted him as saying EMU should start without Italy since Rome would flunk a mandatory criteria for membership which limits the size of national budget deficits.

After Prodi's comments, Germany's Juergen Stark, state secretary in the finance ministry, said Tuesday he knew of no plans aimed at keeping Italy out of the first group of nations. His remarks had little market impact, dealers said.
In other trading, the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3547 from C$1.3517.
